nameStory: Angel's-tears gets its poetic name from the delicate, drooping white flowers that hang like tiny teardrops from slender stems. The nodding blooms seem to weep gracefully in spring breezes, creating an almost ethereal appearance in the garden. This touching name captures the flower's gentle, melancholy beauty perfectly.
description: Angel's-tears is a charming small daffodil that produces clusters of pure white, bell-shaped flowers that gracefully nod downward like tiny hanging lanterns. This bulb plant typically grows 6-8 inches tall with narrow, grass-like leaves that emerge from the ground in early spring. Unlike the bold, upright trumpet daffodils most people know, Angel's-tears has a delicate, woodland fairy quality with its petite stature and drooping white blooms. It's primarily grown as an ornamental garden plant and is quite rare in New England's wild spaces.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers hang downward like tiny bells, usually 2-6 per stem, with swept-back petals and a small cup-shaped center that feels papery to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing bulb plant reaching only 6-8 inches tall, much shorter than common daffodils, with flowers that nod or droop rather than face upward

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, strap-shaped leaves that feel smooth and slightly waxy, emerging directly from the ground in small clumps of 3-5 leaves

idTips.label: Bloom Pattern
idTips.description: Multiple small flowers cluster at the top of each thin stem, creating a graceful weeping effect as they all hang downward

habitat: Angel's-tears is almost exclusively found in cultivated gardens, rock gardens, and naturalized areas around old home sites in New England. It prefers well-drained soil and partial shade, often planted under deciduous trees or in woodland garden settings. With only one recorded observation in all of New England, this is clearly a rare garden escape rather than a naturalized wildflower.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in early spring followed by drooping white flowers in April to May, creating the plant's most distinctive and identifiable stage.
seasonality.summer: Foliage remains green through late spring but dies back by midsummer, leaving no trace above ground for the rest of the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Completely dormant with no visible parts above ground, existing only as a bulb underground.
seasonality.winter: Dormant bulb stage with no visible growth, though bulbs may begin developing shoots late in the season under snow cover.

funFact: The popular garden variety 'Hawera' has won the Royal Horticultural Society's prestigious Award of Garden Merit, yet Angel's-tears remains so rare in New England that there's only been a single documented sighting across all six states combined!
confusionNotes: Angel's-tears might be confused with other small white spring bulbs like snowdrops, but snowdrops bloom much earlier (often through snow) and have only single flowers per stem. The drooping, clustered flowers and daffodil family features make Angel's-tears unique once you know what to look for.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a daffodil, Angel's-tears looks nothing like the classic yellow trumpet daffodils most people picture. All plants in the Narcissus genus are technically daffodils, but they come in surprising variety of sizes, colors, and flower forms. This species represents the delicate, woodland end of the daffodil spectrum.
compareHints: Angel's-tears differs from other New England daffodils by its tiny size, pure white color, and distinctly drooping flowers. Wild daffodil and Poet's narcissus are much taller with upward-facing blooms, while Paperwhite has upright clusters and Bunch-flowered daffodil has yellow centers. The nodding, bell-like white flowers make Angel's-tears unmistakable among its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the familiar yellow trumpet daffodils (Narcissus pseudonarcissus) that bloom earlier, poet's narcissus has pure white petals and a flat, small center rather than a large trumpet.

Wild daffodil differs from its Narcissus relatives by having pale yellow petals rather than the pure white of Poet's Narcissus or Paperwhite, and produces single flowers rather than the clusters seen in Bunch-flowered Daffodil.
Unlike wild daffodil which has one large flower per stem, this species always has multiple smaller flowers clustered together.

Unlike other daffodils in New England, the hoop-petticoat has an enormous corona that completely dominates tiny, thread-like petals - the exact opposite of poet's narcissus which has huge white petals and a tiny orange cup.
Unlike other New England daffodils that bloom singly in spring with thick, substantial petals, paperwhite produces clusters of smaller flowers with distinctively thin, translucent petals.
